It's the author using vague language to try to establish that their research is what's called "generalizable." In science, if a study or result has applications outside the lab, then it's considered "generalizable" (aka, of practical value). Examples of science which aren't generalizable would be things like what's called "basic science," where you're determining fundamental laws of nature (which is still crucially important, it just doesn't have immediate practical significance), or maybe some behavioral study whose results don't apply except for absurdly specific conditions that will never occur outside a professor's lab. Frankly, I haven't read the study - can't access it, thanks Elsevier /s - so this may very well fall within the latter category.

If, however, the study is generalizable, then you could use it to draw conclusions about fats in natural settings and circumstances, and whether or not they should be there. For instance, assuming that the study is correct and that you want just and less corrupt social systems, don't put fats in positions of power. Or trivial positions. Or associate with them at all, really.

This study looks great, but the response to it is kind of grinding my gears. This study doesn't "prove" anything. A single study is not able to prove something in science, especially in social science. This study is solely an observation: a group of researchers reached for something they could call a "phenomenon" and found it. There are hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions of those every year. Most of them accomplish nothing. This one looks like - I can't read it, unfortunately - it found something worthy of another study.

It's still, at best, an observation, the first step in the scientific method. If proven valid (it still needs to be peer reviewed and reproduced a couple times), this observation might yield a hypothesis, only then we'll have something that can be asserted (or rejected). Even then, it won't become proven, but it will hold scientific value to the rest of the academic community.

Please refrain from using it as an argument against FA/HAES obeasts. Focus on what's scientifically established time and time again: obesity is unhealthy and disgusting, becoming obese denotes laziness and lack of self-control, glorifying obesity is assisted suicide.
